questions.prompt: Walk through the read path from a product-listing URL to the Spree catalog request in MasterStore: which function owns each transformation, what does the URL parser actually promise, and what happens to a query-string value it does not accept?

keyPoints.text: [w2] The server page awaits searchParams (a record of string, string[] or undefined) and hands it whole to parseListingSearchParams; readFirst takes element 0 of an array or URLSearchParams.get, while readAll keeps every repeat, which is how repeated option params survive.
[w2] The parser's job is narrow: it decides whether caller-supplied text becomes a filter value at all, and passing that test does not make the value trustworthy downstream.
keyPoints.quote: Parsing it is different from trusting it.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Rejection is by omission: each accepted bound, availability or sort is added through a conditional spread, so a refused value leaves no key in the filters object rather than an error or a sentinel.

[w2] Pagination is deliberately not part of the URL contract: listings use infinite scroll, so the count of pages scrolled lives in the client island and resets whenever filters, sort or query change.

[w3] buildProductQueryParams is the translation layer to Spree's vocabulary: search, price_gte/price_lte, with_option_value_ids, an in_stock or out_of_stock boolean, and sort unless it is manual; the SDK then wraps these flat keys in Ransack q[...] for products.list.

[w2] Route-owned constraints beat caller input by spread order: the category page passes baseParams { in_category: category.id }, which ProductListing spreads after the URL-derived params (and fields after both), so nothing in the query string can point a category listing at another category.

[w1] The inverse direction shares the contract: buildListingSearchParams rewrites only the listing-owned keys and copies every other param from the base URL, so the client filter controls and the server parse use one key vocabulary.

questions.prompt: Explain the seam between the Next.js storefront and the Spree API on catalog reads: how the API client comes into existence, what decides whether two listing requests share one cached response, and how long a catalog change in Spree can stay invisible to shoppers.

keyPoints.text: [w3] getClient is a lazily built module-level singleton: on first use it reads SPREE_API_URL and SPREE_PUBLISHABLE_KEY, and if either is missing it throws a configuration error at request time instead of failing the boot.

[w3] cachedListProducts is a 'use cache: remote' function, so its arguments are the cache identity: the SDK params, the locale/country options and a trailing token argument that the body never forwards to Spree; signed-in shoppers get their own entries and all guests share one.

[w2] Locale and country come from cookies the middleware set, falling back to the configured defaults, including during prerendering when cookies() rejects; they shape both the request and the cache entry.

[w3] Freshness is time-bound only: the tenMinutes profile is stale 300s, revalidate 600s, expire 3600s, and nothing in storefront/src invalidates the products tag (updateTag is only called for cart, checkout, addresses, customer and credit-card data), so a Spree price edit waits out the window.

[w2] The listing pins fields to PRODUCT_CARD_FIELDS as the last spread, so neither the filter params nor a category's baseParams can widen the payload; a smaller response means a smaller cached entry and a smaller RSC stream.

[w2] The facet-count fetch drops sort from its arguments because counts do not depend on order, so a sort change reuses the filters entry instead of minting a new one; its flat keys are wrapped into Ransack q[...] form by hand right before that fetch.

questions.prompt: Defend or indict the error contract of the listing read path: what does a shopper see when the first product page fails, when the facet request fails, when a later infinite-scroll page fails, and when a filter value is malformed, and why is each failure routed where it is?

keyPoints.text: [w3] The first products fetch is deliberately left uncaught so a Spree outage or bad request reaches the error boundary (the app has only global-error.tsx, which reports to Sentry and offers a retry) instead of rendering as a believable 'no products found'.
[w2] Facet data is treated as cosmetic: its promise has a .catch that logs and yields null, and the filter bar renders without counts while the grid still shows.

[w3] A failed load-more flips a separate hasError flag rather than touching the page count, so failure is not mistaken for 'exhausted': the observer gate stops re-firing in a hot loop and the end-of-list message stays hidden until a filter change remounts the island or the page is refreshed.
[w2] Appended pages are de-duplicated by product id, so a catalog that shifts between page requests does not double a card, and the known page count is refreshed from each response.

[w2] A malformed bound also drops out of the URL on its own: it stays in the address bar until the shopper changes any filter, then the filter bar rebuilds every listing-owned key from the parsed state, which never held it.

[w2] Contrast the mutation side: server actions there return a { success, error } envelope via actionResult or swallow to a fallback via withFallback, while the catalog read throws, because an empty catalog is a legitimate answer that must not hide an outage.
